title: Tax-Advantaged Accounts and Products

brief.h: Tax deferral and the plan map
brief.md:
- **Tax-deferred growth**: no tax each year on dividends, interest or capital gains inside the account; **100% of earnings are reinvested** (compounding). Tax is due only when money is **distributed**.
- Taxable retirement distributions are **always ordinary income, never capital gains**.
- Accounts covered in this chapter: **corporate plans** (qualified / non-qualified), **IRAs** (traditional / Roth), **annuities**, **529 plans**, **Coverdell ESAs**, **ABLE accounts**.

| Account | Contributions | Growth | Distributions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qualified plan** (401(k), pension…) | **Pre-tax** (deductible) | Tax-deferred | **All** taxed as ordinary income |
| **Non-qualified plan** | **After-tax** (non-deductible) | Tax-deferred | **Only growth** taxed as ordinary income |
| **Traditional IRA (deductible)** | Pre-tax | Tax-deferred | All taxable (works like qualified) |
| **Traditional IRA (non-deductible)** | After-tax | Tax-deferred | Only growth taxable (works like non-qualified) |
| **Roth IRA** | After-tax | Tax-deferred | **Tax-free** if qualified |
| **529 / ABLE / Coverdell** | After-tax | Tax-free | **Tax-free** if used for qualified expenses |

> **Exam tip** Ask two questions: *were contributions pre-tax or after-tax?* Pre-tax = everything taxed on the way out. After-tax = only the growth is taxed (or nothing at all for Roth/529/ABLE).

- **Qualified corporate plan** = meets **ERISA** guidelines → employer and employee make **pre-tax (tax-deductible)** contributions; growth is tax-deferred; **all distributions are ordinary income**.
- **ERISA** (Employee Retirement Income Security Act, **1974**) protects **private-sector** workers. It does **not** apply to government employees’ plans, and not to IRAs (individual plans).
- ERISA requirements:
  1. At least one **fiduciary** who must act in the participants’ best interest.
  2. **Non-discrimination**: no one can be screened out if they are a **full-time employee who has reached 21 and completed one year of service**; a **part-timer logging 500+ hours three years in a row** must also be admitted.
  3. A **vesting schedule** for employer contributions.
- **Vesting**: ownership of employer contributions. Vested benefits **cannot be taken away** (bankruptcy, dismissal). **Employee’s own contributions are vested immediately (100%)**; employer contributions must be **100% vested after five years** of service at the latest.
- Sample schedule: year 1 = 0%, year 2 = 50%, year 3 = 100%.
- An individual **can contribute to both** a corporate plan and an IRA.
> **Exam tip** “Fully vested in two years” means a right to **all employer contributions** after two years, not eligibility and not tax-free withdrawals.

| | **Defined benefit** (pension) | **Defined contribution** |
|---|---|---|
| Promise | **Specified retirement income** (dollar amount or formula of salary, age, years of service) | **No minimum benefit** |
| Funding | **100% employer** | Employer and **employee** |
| Accounts | **No individual accounts** – one trust, professionally managed | **Individual accounts** |
| Investment risk | **Employer** (must add money if returns fall short) | **Employee** |
| Retirement income depends on | Formula (grows with **years of service**) | Contributions + investment performance |
| Actuary | **Yes** – calculates required annual contributions | No |
| Examples | **Pension plan** | 401(k), profit-sharing, SEP, SIMPLE, Keogh, 403(b), 457(b) |

- Defined benefit risk: **underfunded** plan (assets < promised benefits).
- Complexity and cost → many employers dropped DB plans; the trend is toward **defined contribution**.
- Defined contribution plans meet ERISA, so they are **all qualified**: deductible contributions, tax-deferred growth, distributions taxed as ordinary income.
- Both types: ERISA-covered, earnings tax-deferred.
> **Exam tip** *Who bears the investment risk?* DB = employer. DC = employee.

- **401(k)**: most popular employer plan. Employee **elective deferral** of salary instead of cash pay; participants **direct their own investments**. Employer match is **optional** (employers are not required to contribute at all).
  - Match example: employer matches 50% of deferrals up to 5% of pay. Pay $100,000, defer $10,000 → match = 50% × $5,000 = **$2,500**; total in = **$12,500**.
- **Roth 401(k)** (allowed since **2006**, optional for employer): mirrors a Roth IRA but sits inside the plan; **only employee deferrals**, made **after-tax**; **employer match always goes to the regular 401(k)**. Distributions tax-free if **5 years** since first Roth deferral **and age 59½**.
- **Profit-sharing**: employer contribution **varies with profits**; the **same percentage of pay** for all eligible employees; often combined with a 401(k). Difference from 401(k): the 401(k) adds the employee’s **option to contribute** own money.
- **Keogh (HR-10)**: for **self-employed** persons / unincorporated business owners (and their employees). Seldom set up today. *Exam: self-employed only.*
- **SEP-IRA**: small-business plan, cheap to run; contributions go into each participant’s IRA; **employer only** (employees cannot contribute); optional for employer; **same percentage** for all eligible employees.
- **SIMPLE IRA**: companies with **100 employees or fewer**; **employer contributions required**; employees **may** defer salary.
> **Exam tip** SEP = employer only. SIMPLE = employer required, employee optional, 100 or fewer.

- **403(b)** (tax-sheltered annuity, **TSA**): for **public schools, 501(c)(3) charities and certain religious institutions**; elective deferrals like a 401(k); contributions are **tax-deductible**.
- **457(b)**: **deferred compensation** plans of **state/local governments and tax-exempt 501(c) organizations**; participant-directed; same tax treatment and contribution limits as 401(k)/403(b).
- **Non-qualified plans** (not ERISA): payroll deduction plans, deferred compensation plans.
  - Advantages for employer: choose **which employees** participate, reward key executives more, **no nondiscrimination tests**, **no contribution limit**.
  - Contributions are **after-tax / non-deductible** to the company; employee owes tax at distribution; company deducts when benefits are paid.
  - Growth tax-deferred; at distribution **only the growth** is taxed as ordinary income (example: $500,000 funded → $700,000 = **$200,000 taxable**).
  - **Credit risk**: benefits can be lost if the company changes its mind, is acquired, or goes **bankrupt** (assets reachable by creditors).
  - Employees have **no automatic eligibility** – the employer decides.
> **Exam tip** For non-qualified plans the exam only needs: **after-tax contributions** and **credit risk if the employer is insolvent**.

brief.h: Traditional IRA: contributions and tax treatment
brief.md:
- Open to anyone with **earned income** (wages, salary, commissions; self-employment income counts). **No minimum age** and no maximum age to contribute. Held in **one person’s name**, never joint.
- **Limit (2026)**: the **lesser of $7,500 or 100% of earned income**. Age **50+**: **$1,100 catch-up** → **$8,600**.
- **Excess contribution**: **6% penalty** on the excess.
- **Not earned income**: capital gains, dividends, interest, pension income. Only investment income = **no IRA contribution** (traditional or Roth).
- **Spousal IRA**: a working spouse can fund a **separate** IRA for a non-working spouse. Example: John 52 earns all $80,000 → $8,600 to his own, $7,500 to Helen (48).
- **Deadline**: the due date of the next federal tax return, usually **April 15** (2022 contributions until April 15, 2023).
- Multiple IRAs (traditional + Roth): the limit applies to **all combined**.
- **Prohibited investments**: **fixed life insurance**, **antiques/collectibles** (except certain US gold and silver coins), **risky options** such as uncovered calls, **real estate** (direct). Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, REITs are fine.
- **Deductibility**: 
  1. Not eligible for an employer plan → **pre-tax** (deductible).
  2. Eligible for an employer plan but income **below** a threshold → pre-tax.
  3. Eligible for an employer plan and income **above** the threshold → **after-tax** (non-deductible).
- Pre-tax IRA: all distributions taxed as ordinary income. After-tax IRA: only **earnings** taxed (distribution above basis).
> **Exam tip** Exact income thresholds are *not* tested. Know the three scenarios and that deductible IRA = qualified plan, non-deductible IRA = non-qualified plan.

brief.h: Traditional IRA: distributions, exceptions, rollovers, RMDs
brief.md:
- Penalty-free withdrawals start at **age 59½**. Before that: **10% penalty** (on top of ordinary income tax) unless an exception applies.
- **Exceptions to the 10% penalty**: **disability**; **education** expenses (owner, spouse, children, grandchildren); **first-time homebuyer** (limit **$10,000**); **medical** expenses; **death** of owner; **birth/adoption** (limit **$5,000 per parent**); **terminally ill**; federally declared **disaster area** (up to **$22,000**).
  - Example: age 55, withdraws $20,000 deductible money → $20,000 added to income + **$2,000** penalty.
  - An exception removes the **penalty**, not the income tax.
- **Rollover** from one IRA provider to another: complete within **60 days** to avoid tax and penalty.
- **RMDs**: begin by **April 1 of the year after turning 73** (the required beginning date, RBD); later RMDs by **December 31** each year; book notes the age rises to **75 in 2033**.
  - Amount = account value ÷ IRS life-expectancy factor → **bigger balance = bigger RMD**.
  - Continue **every year for life** or until depleted; owner may take more than required.
  - **Penalty for missing**: **25% excise tax** on the shortfall, reduced to **10%** if corrected within **two years**. Example: RMD $10,000 missed → **$2,500**.
  - RMDs exist so the IRS can tax money that was sheltered.
> **Exam tip** Early-withdrawal penalty = **10%**, missed-RMD penalty = **25%**, excess-contribution penalty = **6%**. Do not swap them.

- **Same as traditional**: $7,500 limit (+$1,100 catch-up at 50+), 100% of earned income cap, same investment choices and **same prohibited investments**, tax-deferred growth, aggregate limit across all IRAs.
- **Different**:
  - **Income limit** to contribute (exact numbers not tested) – above it, no contribution.
  - Contributions **always after-tax** (never deductible).
  - **Qualified distributions are tax-free**, including growth.
  - **No RMDs during the owner’s lifetime**; the RMD requirement is triggered by the owner’s **death**.
  - Not affected by being covered by a **workplace plan**; **no age limit** to contribute (with earned income).
- **Qualified distribution** needs both: (1) **5-year period** starting with the **first tax year** a Roth was established; (2) owner **at least 59½**.
  - Example: opened Nov 14, 2012 → year 1 = 2012 … year 5 = 2016 → qualified from **Jan 1, 2017** if 59½.
- **Non-qualified distribution**: contributions come out tax-free; **earnings** are taxable and subject to the 10% penalty **unless** an exception applies.
- Under 59½ with a valid exception and **under 5 years**: **no 10% penalty but earnings are taxed**. Open 5+ years: earnings not taxed either.
- Roth IRA and 529 plan: **same tax consequences** (after-tax in, tax-free growth, tax-free out when requirements met).
> **Exam tip** Roth: *no RMD* until death. Traditional: RMD by April 1 after turning 73.

brief.h: Annuity basics, general account and fixed annuities
brief.md:
- **Annuity** = insurance contract paying income guaranteed for life of the **annuitant**. Life insurance protects against dying too soon; annuities protect against **living too long**.
- **Deferred** annuity: earnings accumulate until a future date (single premium or periodic payments); longer deferral = bigger payout. **Immediate** annuity: payments start shortly after issue (about one month to one year).
- Growth is **tax-deferred**; tax is paid at distribution.
- **General account**: invests premiums conservatively (Treasuries, high-grade corporate bonds, few equities) to meet **guarantees**; insurer bears risk. Supports **fixed** products.
  - **GIC** (guaranteed investment contract): works like a **time deposit** – fixed period, **guaranteed interest and return of principal**.
- **Separate account**: funds **variable** products; investors pick **subaccounts** (like mutual funds); **investor bears market risk**. Unit values calculated **daily**.
  - Regulated as an **investment company** under the **Investment Company Act of 1940**; also subject to the **Securities Act of 1933** and **Securities Exchange Act of 1934**; its manager falls under the **Investment Advisers Act of 1940**.
- **Fixed annuity**: guaranteed principal and fixed interest; paid from the general account; insurer bears investment risk; **not a security** → **insurance license only**. Greatest risk = **purchasing power (inflation) risk**. Lightly tested.
> **Exam tip** Fixed = general account = not a security. Variable = separate account = security.

- Return depends on the **separate account** subaccounts → inflation-resistant, potential for higher return, but **investor bears risk**. A **security**: SEC registration, **prospectus**, and the seller needs **both insurance and securities licenses**.
- **Accumulation phase**: owner pays in; premiums buy **accumulation units** of a subaccount; number of units rises with more money invested and **unit value fluctuates** (recalculated daily). **Guaranteed death benefit**: beneficiary gets the **greater of current value or amount contributed** (ends at annuitization). Example: $100,000 invested; value $150,000 → $150,000; value $80,000 → $100,000.
- **Annuitization phase**: accumulation units convert to a **fixed number of annuity units**; **unit value varies**, so each payment can differ, but **payments continue for life**.
- **Payout options** (chosen before annuitization; **irrevocable**):

| Option | Beneficiary protection | Monthly payment |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight life** | None – stops at death | **Highest** |
| **Life with period certain** (10 or 15 years) | Only during the period certain | Middle |
| **Joint with last survivor** | Continues until second annuitant dies | **Lowest** |

- **Surrender charge**: back-end sales charge on withdrawals within **6–10 years**, % of amount withdrawn, **declining** yearly (example 9% year 1 down to 0% in year 10+). Recoups rep commission; reduces liquidity.
- **Taxation**: most contributions are **after-tax** → tax on withdrawal = **value − basis**. Annuity inside a qualified plan (e.g., 403(b), pre-tax) → **all distributions taxable**. Before **59½**: **10% penalty on earnings**.
- **Suitability (FINRA Rule 2330)**: rep needs reason to believe customer benefits and the customer was told about surrender charges, 59½ tax penalty, subaccount fees, rep sales charges, insurance and investment components (death benefit, separate account) and **market risk**. Costly → for **long-term** investors.
- **1035 exchange**: tax-free transfer from one annuity contract to another; **surrender charges may still apply**.
> **Exam tip** Straight life = highest check, joint last survivor = lowest. Death benefit = **greater of** value or contributions.

- **Municipal fund securities** issued by **states**; all states offer them. Open in **any** state; beneficiary need not attend school there.
- **Who**: any **adult** can open and contribute; beneficiary need not be a relative but must be an **existing child** (not unborn). **No earned income** required. A parent can open one for **themselves** if used for qualified education expenses.
- **Contributions after-tax**; **maximum varies by state**. Owner keeps **control** (including investment selection) until money is spent.
- **Change beneficiary** anytime without tax **if the new beneficiary is a family member**; unused funds can move to a family member’s 529 once per year with no penalty. No age limit on a 529 beneficiary.
- **Investment options**: **age-based** (more conservative as college nears), **risk-based** (static), **guaranteed/insured** (protect principal).
- **Sold**: **adviser-sold** (through municipal securities firms) vs **direct-sold** (directly with the plan; often lower fees but no advice).
- **Prepaid tuition plans**: lock in tuition at designated (often in-state public) colleges; much less popular.
- **Qualified expenses**: tuition, books, supplies, equipment, technology and internet fees, special-needs expenses (the **school must require** the expense); **room and board only if enrolled at least half-time** and up to the school’s allowance. **K-12: up to $20,000 per year** (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, 2017). **Student loans: up to $10,000** (SECURE Act, 2020).
- **Federal tax**: after-tax in, growth tax-free, qualified distributions **tax-free**. **Non-qualified** distributions: **ordinary income tax (on earnings) plus 10% federal penalty**.
- **State tax**: some states give a **deduction** for in-state contributions; some penalize out-of-state plans (state tax on growth). MSRB rules require disclosing out-of-state tax consequences **at or before the sale**.
> **Exam tip** 529 and Roth IRA share the same tax pattern. Contributions are **never** federally deductible.

brief.h: Coverdell ESA, ABLE accounts and MSRB reporting
brief.md:
- **Coverdell ESA**: *not* a municipal fund security; same tax treatment as a 529 (after-tax in, tax-free growth, tax-free for qualified education expenses from **K-12 through college**).
  - Limit **$2,000 per beneficiary per year**; available only to families **below an income level**.
  - Open for a student **under 18**; unspent money must be used or **moved to a family member before the beneficiary reaches 30**, otherwise **income tax + 10% penalty**.
  - Far less popular than a 529 because of the low limit.
- **ABLE account** (Achieving a Better Life Experience Act, **2014**): tax-advantaged savings for **individuals with disabilities**; municipal fund security; available in all states.
  - Eligible only if the disability began **before age 46**.
  - **After-tax** contributions, **tax-free growth**, **tax-free** distributions at federal level for qualified disability expenses (education, housing, transportation, employment support/training, health and wellness).
  - Same contribution limits, tax treatment and reporting rules as 529s; supplements private insurance and social benefits.
- **MSRB Rule G-45**: **underwriters** of 529 plans and ABLE programs must submit data electronically to the MSRB **semiannually**: (1) **plan description** (state, plan name, manager), (2) **aggregate plan information** (total assets, contributions, distributions), (3) **investment option information** (options, objectives, underlying investments with allocations, expenses, performance). **Does not apply to LGIPs**.
> **Exam tip** Coverdell = $2,000, under 18, age 30. ABLE = disability before 46. 529 = no age limit.

traps: **Qualified vs non-qualified taxation.** Qualified = pre-tax in, **everything** taxed as ordinary income out. Non-qualified = after-tax in, **only the growth** taxed out. The Robin example: $500,000 funded, $700,000 value → $200,000 taxable.

**Defined benefit vs defined contribution.** Pension = defined benefit, employer funds 100% and bears investment risk. 401(k) = defined contribution, employee bears the risk. Actuaries belong to DB plans only.
**ERISA scope.** ERISA covers private-sector employer plans. It does not cover government workers’ plans, and traditional/Roth IRAs are individual accounts outside it.
**Vesting of whose money.** An employee’s own contributions are **always 100% vested immediately**. Only employer contributions follow a vesting schedule (100% by year five at the latest).

**SEP vs SIMPLE.** SEP: employer-only contributions, optional for the employer, same percentage for everyone. SIMPLE: employer contribution **required**, employees may also defer, 100 employees or fewer.
**401(k) vs profit-sharing.** The 401(k) adds the employee’s elective deferral. Neither forces the employer to contribute; profit-sharing amounts vary with company profits.
**Keogh.** For exam purposes it is for the **self-employed only**, not for any small corporation.
**Roth 401(k) match.** Employer matching contributions never go into the Roth account; they go to the regular (pre-tax) 401(k) account.

**Earned vs investment income.** IRA contributions need **earned income** (wages, salary, commissions). Dividends, interest, capital gains and pension income do not count, and this applies to Roth and traditional alike.
**Lesser of, not greater of.** The IRA limit is the **lesser** of $7,500 or 100% of earned income. A student earning $4,000 can contribute $4,000.
**Three IRA penalties.** Excess contribution = 6% of the excess. Early withdrawal before 59½ = 10% of the withdrawal. Missed RMD = 25% of the shortfall (10% if fixed within two years).
**RMD start vs RMD for Roth.** Traditional IRA: first RMD by April 1 after the year the owner turns 73. Roth IRA: no RMD during the owner’s lifetime – the requirement is triggered by death.
**Penalty exception does not erase tax.** An exception (disability, education, medical…) waives the **10% penalty** only; a deductible traditional IRA withdrawal is still ordinary income.

**Roth five-year clock.** The clock starts with the **first tax year** a Roth was established (even a late-in-the-year opening, like the book’s November example, counts as year one). Both the five years **and** age 59½ are needed for tax-free earnings.

**Fixed vs variable annuity.** Fixed: general account, insurer bears risk, not a security, insurance license only, inflation (purchasing power) risk. Variable: separate account, investor bears risk, security, both licenses and a prospectus.
**General account vs separate account.** General account = conservative investments backing guarantees. Separate account = market-based subaccounts, regulated as an investment company.

**Accumulation units vs annuity units.** Accumulation units are bought during the accumulation phase; at annuitization they convert into a **fixed number** of annuity units whose value (and the monthly check) varies.

**Payout option ranking.** Straight life pays the **most** but leaves nothing to a beneficiary; joint with last survivor pays the **least**. Life with period certain protects the beneficiary only during the period.
**Variable annuity death benefit.** The beneficiary receives the **greater** of current value or amount contributed, and only if death occurs before annuitization.
**1035 exchange.** Tax-free, but it does not necessarily avoid **surrender charges**.

**529 vs Coverdell vs ABLE.** 529: no age limit, state-set maximums, K-12 up to $20,000/yr. Coverdell: $2,000/yr, income limits, assets by age 30. ABLE: disability onset before age 46. All three: after-tax in, tax-free growth.
**529 non-qualified withdrawal.** Earnings are taxed as ordinary income **plus** a 10% federal penalty. State rules may also tax growth, especially for out-of-state plans.

formulas.name: Tax treatment decision rule
formulas.rule: Pre-tax contributions (qualified plan, deductible IRA) → **100% of distributions** taxed as ordinary income.  After-tax contributions (non-qualified plan, non-deductible IRA, variable annuity) → taxable = **distribution − basis**.  Roth IRA / 529 / ABLE / Coverdell (qualified) → **$0 taxable**.
formulas.example: Non-qualified plan funded with $500,000 grows to $700,000: taxable = 700,000 − 500,000 = **$200,000**. Qualified plan with $80,000 contributed, $150,000 distributed: taxable = **$150,000**.

formulas.name: IRA contribution limit
formulas.rule: Limit = **lesser of $7,500 or 100% of earned income**; age 50+: add **$1,100** (max $8,600). Spousal IRA: a working spouse may fund a separate IRA for a non-working spouse (combined contributions cannot exceed combined earned income). Excess → **6%**.
formulas.example: Married couple, only the husband (age 52) works and earns $80,000; wife is 48. Husband: 7,500 + 1,100 = **$8,600**. Wife’s spousal IRA: **$7,500**. If he earned only $5,000 total, the couple could contribute at most $5,000 combined.

formulas.name: Early withdrawal cost
formulas.rule: Before 59½ (no exception): **tax on taxable portion at ordinary rates + 10% × amount withdrawn**. With an exception: tax only. Qualified distribution after 59½: tax only (traditional) / none (Roth, if 5 years).
formulas.example: Age 45 withdraws $30,000 pre-tax IRA money for a car: income +$30,000 and penalty 10% × 30,000 = **$3,000**. If the money paid her child’s tuition: penalty **$0**, still taxable.

formulas.name: RMD shortfall excise tax
formulas.rule: Excise tax = **25% × (RMD − amount actually taken)**; reduced to **10%** if corrected in the next two years. First RMD by **April 1** after the year of the 73rd birthday; later ones by December 31.
formulas.example: RMD $16,000, owner takes $6,000 → shortfall $10,000 → excise tax 25% × 10,000 = **$2,500** (or $1,000 at the 10% rate if corrected in time).

formulas.name: Roth IRA qualified-distribution test
formulas.rule: Tax-free if **both**: (1) after the 5-year period beginning with the **first tax year** of any Roth IRA; and (2) owner is **59½ or older**. Count the opening year as year 1.
formulas.example: Roth opened January 30, 2018: 2018 = yr 1, 2019 = 2, 2020 = 3, 2021 = 4, 2022 = 5 → qualified from **January 1, 2023** (if already 59½).

formulas.name: 401(k) match arithmetic
formulas.rule: Match = match % × the **lesser of** the employee’s deferral or the matched cap (% of pay). Total annual addition = deferral + match.

formulas.name: Variable annuity death benefit and surrender charge
formulas.rule: Death benefit (before annuitization) = **greater of** current account value or total contributions.  Surrender charge = **schedule % for the year × amount withdrawn**.
formulas.example: Contributions $120,000; value $95,000 at death → beneficiary receives **$120,000**. Withdrawing $20,000 in year 4 of a 9-8-7-6… schedule: 6% × 20,000 = **$1,200**.

formulas.name: Annuity payout option ranking
formulas.rule: Monthly payment: **Straight life (highest) > Life with period certain > Joint with last survivor (lowest)**. Beneficiary protection moves in the opposite direction.
formulas.example: Same $500,000 balance: straight life might pay the largest check but stops at death; joint with last survivor pays the smallest check but continues until the second annuitant dies.
