A 529 plan purchased through an authorized municipal securities firm.
A 529 plan purchased directly from the plan, often with lower fees and no advice.
A plan that lets families prepay future tuition at designated colleges.
Tuition, books, supplies, required equipment and fees, and room and board for half-time students at an eligible institution.
An education savings account with a $2,000 annual limit, income limits and a deadline to use funds by age 30.
A tax-advantaged savings account for individuals whose disability began before age 46.
Requires 529 and ABLE program underwriters to report plan data to the MSRB twice a year.
The risk that fixed annuity payments will not keep up with inflation.

cards.f: What does tax-deferred growth mean?
cards.b: No tax each year on dividends, interest or gains; tax is due only at **distribution**, so 100% of earnings stay invested.

cards.f: Taxable retirement distributions are taxed as…
cards.b: **Ordinary income**, never capital gains.

cards.f: Qualified plan: contribution and distribution tax treatment
cards.b: **Pre-tax** contributions; **all** distributions taxed as ordinary income.

cards.f: Non-qualified plan: contribution and distribution tax treatment
cards.b: **After-tax** contributions; only the **growth** is taxed as ordinary income at distribution.

cards.f: What does ERISA cover?
cards.b: **Private-sector** employer-sponsored plans. Not government employees’ plans, not IRAs.

cards.f: Year ERISA was passed
Three ERISA plan requirements
cards.b: At least one **fiduciary**; **non-discrimination** in eligibility; a **vesting schedule** for employer contributions.

cards.f: ERISA eligibility: who must be allowed in?
cards.b: Full-time employees **age 21 with one year of service**; part-timers with **500+ hours in three consecutive years**.

cards.f: Vesting of the employee’s own contributions
cards.b: **Immediately 100% vested**.

cards.f: Maximum vesting delay for employer contributions
cards.b: Full (**100%**) vesting is required no later than **five years** of service.

cards.f: Can vested benefits be lost in an employer bankruptcy?
cards.b: **No** – vested benefits cannot be taken away (bankruptcy, dismissal).

cards.f: Defined benefit plan: who funds it and who bears investment risk?
cards.b: **100% employer**-funded; the **employer** bears all investment risk.

cards.f: Which professional sets the annual funding for a pension?
cards.b: An **actuary**.

cards.f: Does a defined benefit plan have individual employee accounts?
cards.b: **No** – assets sit in one professionally managed trust.

cards.f: What is an underfunded pension plan?
cards.b: Assets are **not enough** to pay promised retirement obligations.

cards.f: Defined contribution plan: what determines retirement income?
cards.b: Amount **contributed** plus **investment performance**; no minimum benefit is promised.

cards.f: Are all defined contribution plans qualified?
cards.b: **Yes** – they meet ERISA: deductible contributions, tax-deferred growth, distributions taxed as ordinary income.

cards.f: Most popular employer-sponsored retirement plan
cards.b: The **401(k)** (a defined contribution plan).

cards.f: Is an employer match required in a 401(k)?
cards.b: **No** – matching and profit-sharing contributions are optional.

cards.f: Employer matches 50% of deferrals up to 5% of pay. Pay $100,000, deferral $10,000. Match?
Roth 401(k): which contributions go in the Roth account?
cards.b: Only **employee** deferrals (after-tax); the **employer match goes to the regular 401(k)**.

cards.f: Roth 401(k) tax-free distribution conditions
cards.b: At least **5 years** after first Roth deferral **and** age **59½**.

cards.f: Profit-sharing plan key feature
cards.b: Employer varies contributions with **profits**; same **percentage of pay** for all eligible employees.

cards.f: Keogh (HR-10) plan: who is it for?
cards.b: **Self-employed** individuals and unincorporated business owners only.

cards.f: Who may contribute to a SEP-IRA?
cards.b: **Only the employer**, never the employee; same percentage for all eligible employees.

cards.f: SIMPLE IRA: size limit and who contributes?
cards.b: Companies with **100 or fewer employees**; employer contributions **required**, employee deferrals optional.

cards.f: 403(b) plan: who sponsors it and its other name?
cards.b: Nonprofits, public schools, 501(c)(3) charities, certain religious institutions; also called a **tax-sheltered annuity (TSA)**.

cards.f: 457(b) plan sponsors
cards.b: **State/local governments** and tax-exempt 501(c) organizations; works like 401(k)/403(b) with the same limits.

cards.f: Why do employers like non-qualified plans?
cards.b: Choose participants, favor executives, **no nondiscrimination tests**, **no contribution limit**.

cards.f: Main risk of a non-qualified plan
cards.b: **Credit risk**: benefits can be lost if the employer is insolvent, acquired or changes its mind; creditors can claim assets.

cards.f: Examples of non-qualified plans
cards.b: **Payroll deduction** plans and **deferred compensation** plans (contributions after-tax).

cards.f: CEO’s non-qualified plan funded with $500,000 grows to $700,000. Taxable at distribution?
cards.b: Only the growth: **$200,000** as ordinary income.

cards.f: Can a person contribute to both a corporate plan and an IRA?
cards.b: **Yes** – holding a workplace plan does not stop a person from also funding an IRA.

cards.f: 2026 traditional IRA contribution limit
cards.b: Lesser of **$7,500** or **100% of earned income**.

cards.f: IRA catch-up contribution
cards.b: **$1,100** extra at age **50+**, for a total of **$8,600**.

cards.f: Penalty for exceeding the IRA contribution limit
cards.b: **6%** of the excess amount.

cards.f: Minimum age to contribute to a traditional IRA
cards.b: **None** – even a child with compensation can contribute.

cards.f: Which income counts for IRA contributions?
cards.b: **Earned income only** (wages, salary, commissions). Not dividends, interest, gains or pension income.

cards.f: Spousal IRA
cards.b: A working spouse funds a **separate** IRA for a non-working spouse; IRAs are never joint.

cards.f: IRA contribution deadline
cards.b: The due date of the next federal tax return, usually **April 15**.

cards.f: Investments prohibited in an IRA
cards.b: Fixed life insurance; antiques/collectibles (except certain US gold/silver coins); risky options such as **uncovered calls**; real estate.

cards.f: When is a traditional IRA contribution pre-tax (deductible)?
cards.b: No employer plan available, **or** employer plan available but income **below** a threshold.

cards.f: When is a traditional IRA contribution after-tax (non-deductible)?
cards.b: Eligible for an employer plan **and** income **above** the threshold.

cards.f: Tax on distributions from a non-deductible traditional IRA
cards.b: Only the **earnings** (amount above basis) are ordinary income; behaves like a non-qualified plan.

cards.f: Age for penalty-free traditional IRA withdrawals
cards.b: **59½**; before that, a **10% penalty** unless an exception applies.

cards.f: Exceptions to the 10% early withdrawal penalty
cards.b: Disability, education, first-time home ($10,000), medical, death, birth/adoption ($5,000 per parent), terminal illness, disaster (up to $22,000).

cards.f: First-time homebuyer exception limit
Birth or adoption exception limit
cards.b: **$5,000 per parent**.

cards.f: Disaster-area exception limit
cards.b: Up to **$22,000** for individuals in federally declared disaster areas.

cards.f: IRA rollover deadline
cards.b: **60 days** to avoid tax liability and the early withdrawal penalty.

cards.f: When must the first traditional IRA RMD be taken?
cards.b: By **April 1 of the year after turning 73** (required beginning date).

cards.f: RMD age scheduled for 2033
cards.b: Rises to **75**.

cards.f: What determines the RMD amount?
cards.b: **Account value** and the owner’s **life expectancy** (IRS tables); larger balance = larger RMD.

cards.f: Penalty for missing an RMD
cards.b: **25% excise tax** on the shortfall; **10%** if corrected within two years.

cards.f: Leonard misses a $10,000 RMD. Penalty at the 25% rate?
Roth IRA vs traditional: contribution limits
cards.b: **Same** limits: $7,500 plus $1,100 catch-up; shared across all IRAs.

cards.f: Roth IRA contributions: tax status
cards.b: Always **after-tax** (non-deductible); only available below an income limit.

cards.f: Roth IRA RMDs
cards.b: **None during the owner’s life**; triggered by the owner’s death.

cards.f: Two tests for a tax-free Roth IRA distribution
cards.b: Taken after the **5-year period** (from first tax year a Roth was opened) **and** after age **59½**.

cards.f: Roth opened in 2012. First tax-free year (assuming 59½)?
cards.b: 2012 is year 1 … 2016 is year 5, so distributions from **January 1, 2017**.

cards.f: Roth, under 59½, valid exception, under 5 years
cards.b: **No 10% penalty**, but the **earnings are taxed**.

cards.f: Roth IRA and 529 plan: what do they share?
cards.b: Same tax pattern: **after-tax in, tax-free growth, tax-free out** when requirements are met.

cards.f: Annuity: what risk does it protect against?
cards.b: **Living too long** (outliving savings); life insurance protects against dying too soon.

cards.f: Deferred vs immediate annuity
cards.b: Deferred: earnings accumulate, payments start later. Immediate: payments begin within about **one month to one year**.

cards.f: Insurance company general account
cards.b: Conservative investments (Treasuries, high-grade bonds) backing **fixed** products; insurer bears the risk.

cards.f: Guaranteed investment contract (GIC)
cards.b: General-account product acting like a **time deposit**: guaranteed interest and principal for a fixed period.

cards.f: Separate account: how is it regulated?
cards.b: As an **investment company** under the **Investment Company Act of 1940**; manager under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.

cards.f: How often are separate account units valued?
cards.b: **Daily**.

cards.f: Fixed annuity: security? license?
cards.b: **Not a security**; seller needs only an **insurance license**.

cards.f: Greatest risk of a fixed annuity
cards.b: **Purchasing power (inflation) risk**.

cards.f: Variable annuity: security? license? document?
cards.b: A **security**: SEC registration, **prospectus**, insurance **and** securities licenses.

cards.f: Accumulation phase: what does the owner buy?
cards.b: **Accumulation units** of a subaccount; unit value is recalculated daily.

cards.f: Variable annuity death benefit (accumulation phase)
cards.b: Beneficiary receives the **greater of** current value or amount contributed.

cards.f: What happens to units at annuitization?
cards.b: Accumulation units convert to a **fixed number of annuity units**; payments vary but last for life.

cards.f: Payout option with the highest monthly payment
cards.b: **Straight life** – nothing goes to a beneficiary at death.

cards.f: Payout option with the lowest monthly payment
cards.b: **Joint with last survivor** – continues until the second annuitant dies.

cards.f: Life with period certain, 10 years; annuitant dies in year 6
cards.b: Beneficiary receives the remaining **4 years** of payments.

cards.f: Can the annuity payout option be changed once it has been chosen?
cards.b: **No** – the choice must be made before annuitization and is final.

cards.f: Surrender charge
cards.b: Back-end sales charge on withdrawals within **6 to 10 years**, a declining % of the amount withdrawn.

cards.f: Variable annuity taxation on withdrawal (after-tax money)
cards.b: Tax on **value minus basis** at ordinary rates; **10% penalty** on earnings before 59½.

cards.f: FINRA rule governing variable annuity suitability
Items a customer must be told before a variable annuity sale
cards.b: Surrender charges, 59½ penalty, subaccount fees, rep sales charges, insurance/investment components, market risk.

cards.f: 1035 exchange
cards.b: **Tax-free** transfer from one annuity contract to another; surrender charges **may still apply**.

cards.f: Who can open a 529 and for whom?
cards.b: Any **adult**, for an **existing child** (not unborn); no earned income needed; beneficiary need not be a relative.

cards.f: Who controls 529 assets?
cards.b: The **account owner**, including investment selection, until the money is withdrawn.

cards.f: Changing a 529 beneficiary
cards.b: Allowed at any time without tax if the new beneficiary is **related** to the old one.

cards.f: 529 age-based vs risk-based options
cards.b: Age-based turns **more conservative** as college nears; risk-based stays in the **same** allocation.

cards.f: Adviser-sold vs direct-sold 529
cards.b: Adviser-sold: through municipal securities firms. Direct-sold: directly with the plan, often lower fees, no advice.

cards.f: When are room and board qualified 529 expenses?
cards.b: Only if enrolled **at least half-time**, up to the school’s allowance.

cards.f: 529 limits for K-12 and student loans
cards.b: **$20,000 per year** for elementary/secondary; **$10,000** toward student loans.

cards.f: 529 non-qualified distribution
cards.b: Earnings taxed as ordinary income **plus a 10% federal penalty**.

cards.f: MSRB duty on out-of-state 529 sales
cards.b: Disclose potential out-of-state **tax consequences** at or before the sale.

cards.f: MSRB Rule G-45 reporting
cards.b: Underwriters of 529/ABLE submit data **semiannually**: plan description, aggregate plan info, investment option info. Not LGIPs.

cards.f: Coverdell ESA key numbers
cards.b: **$2,000** per beneficiary per year; open for student **under 18**; spend or transfer by age **30**.

cards.f: Coverdell funds not used by age 30
cards.b: Subject to federal income tax **plus a 10% penalty**.

cards.f: ABLE account eligibility
cards.b: Disability that began **before age 46**.

cards.f: ABLE account tax pattern
cards.b: **After-tax** contributions, tax-free growth, **tax-free** distributions for qualified disability expenses (same as 529).

cards.f: Why are variable annuities seen as resistant to inflation?
cards.b: Returns follow the market performance of the chosen subaccounts, giving potential for **higher growth** – but the **investor bears the risk**.

cards.f: Prepaid tuition plan
cards.b: Lets families **prepay future tuition** at designated (often in-state public) colleges, sometimes locking in today’s cost; much less popular than savings plans.

cards.f: Defined benefit formula: 1% of average salary × 30 years of service
cards.b: Benefit = **30%** of average salary; benefits rise with **years of service**.

cards.f: Colleague says “I’ll be fully vested in two years.” Meaning?
cards.b: He then has a right to **all employer contributions**; not eligibility, not tax-free withdrawals.

cards.f: Why does a longer deferral period matter in a deferred annuity?
cards.b: More time to accumulate **earnings**, so a **larger potential payout**.

cards.f: When does a company deduct what it spends on a non-qualified plan?
cards.b: Generally **when benefits are distributed**, not when it funds the plan; the employee is taxed then as well.

cards.f: What does a variable annuity prospectus describe?
cards.b: Fees and charges, investment options, death benefits and annuity payout options.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the tax treatment of a qualified corporate retirement plan?
o: Contributions are after-tax and only the growth is taxed at distribution
Contributions are after-tax and all distributions are tax-free
Contributions are pre-tax and distributions are taxed as long-term capital gains
Contributions are pre-tax, growth is tax-deferred, and all distributions are taxed as ordinary income
w: Wrong: this describes a non-qualified plan, where only the growth above the after-tax basis is taxed.
Wrong: tax-free distributions with after-tax contributions describe Roth-type accounts, not qualified corporate plans.
Wrong: retirement plan distributions are never taxed as capital gains, regardless of how the money was earned.
Correct: qualified plans take pre-tax contributions, grow tax-deferred, and every dollar distributed is ordinary income.

questions.q: ERISA protections do NOT extend to which of the following?
o: A 401(k) plan at a private manufacturer
A pension plan at a private bank
A retirement plan covering government employees
A profit-sharing plan at a private company
w: Wrong: a 401(k) sponsored by a private employer is exactly the type of plan ERISA governs.
Wrong: private-sector pension plans are defined benefit plans covered by ERISA.
Correct: ERISA applies to private, employer-sponsored plans only and does not cover plans for government workers.
Wrong: profit-sharing plans at private companies are defined contribution plans subject to ERISA.

questions.q: An employer’s qualified plan vests employer contributions at 0% after year 1, 50% after year 2, and 100% after year 3. Nadia leaves after completing exactly two years. Over that time she contributed $6,000 herself and her employer contributed $18,000. What is the total amount she is entitled to keep?
w: Wrong: $24,000 assumes the employer contributions are fully vested, which does not occur until year three.
Correct: her own $6,000 is immediately 100% vested, plus 50% × $18,000 = $9,000 vested employer money, for $15,000 total.
Wrong: $9,000 is only the vested employer portion and forgets that her own contributions are always hers.
Wrong: $6,000 counts only her own contributions and ignores the 50% of employer money already vested.

questions.q: All of the following are requirements for an ERISA-qualified plan EXCEPT:
o: A mandatory employer matching contribution
A vesting schedule for employer contributions
Non-discriminatory eligibility rules
At least one fiduciary acting in participants’ best interest
w: Correct: ERISA does not force an employer to match; matching contributions are optional.
Wrong: a vesting schedule is one of the three core ERISA requirements.
Wrong: the plan must be offered on a non-discriminatory basis to eligible employees.
Wrong: every ERISA-covered plan must have at least one fiduciary, so this is a genuine requirement.

questions.q: Maria is 23 and works part-time for a private employer that sponsors an ERISA-qualified plan. She has worked 520 hours in each of the last three consecutive years. Which statement is correct?
o: She becomes eligible only after five years of service
She is excluded because only full-time employees may participate
She must wait until age 25 to participate
She must be allowed in, since a part-timer logging 500 or more hours three years in a row must be eligible
w: Wrong: five years is the maximum vesting period for employer money, not an eligibility requirement.
Wrong: the full-time test is only the baseline; qualifying part-timers must also be eligible under ERISA.
Wrong: the age test is 21, not 25, and she is already past it.
Correct: ERISA extends eligibility to part-timers who reach 500 hours in each of three consecutive years.

questions.q:
Which of the following are characteristics of a defined benefit plan?

I. Funded 100% by the employer
II. The employer bears the investment risk
III. Each participant directs investments in an individual account
IV. An actuary determines required contributions
o: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
w: Wrong: this omits item IV, since an actuary calculates the contributions needed to fund promised benefits.
Wrong: item III describes a defined contribution plan, and this pair also leaves out the employer funding.
Correct: defined benefit plans are employer-funded, the employer carries investment risk, and an actuary sets contributions; there are no participant-directed accounts.
Wrong: item III is false because defined benefit plans use a single trust, not participant-directed accounts.

questions.q: In a 401(k) plan, who bears the risk that the investments lose value?
o: The employee
The plan’s actuary
The employer
The plan trustee
w: Correct: 401(k) participants direct their own investments and no minimum benefit is promised, so they bear the risk.
Wrong: actuaries calculate funding for defined benefit plans and do not bear investment risk.
Wrong: employer responsibility for investment results is a feature of defined benefit plans, not 401(k)s.
Wrong: a trustee holds and administers assets but does not guarantee results; with no benefit promised, the participant absorbs the losses.

questions.q: A company’s pension plan investments have performed far below the assumptions used to fund the plan, and the plan is now underfunded. Who must make up the shortfall?
o: The retired participants
The employer
Each active employee through payroll deductions
The plan’s actuary personally
w: Wrong: retirees were promised a specified benefit and do not fund shortfalls in a defined benefit plan.
Correct: the employer carries the entire investment burden and must add money when returns fall short.
Wrong: defined benefit plans are funded entirely by the employer, not by employee payroll deductions.
Wrong: the actuary only calculates the required contributions and has no obligation to fund the plan.

questions.q: Kyle earns $90,000 and defers 8% of his pay into his 401(k). His employer matches 100% of deferrals up to 4% of pay. What is the total amount added to Kyle’s account for the year, ignoring investment earnings?
w: Wrong: $14,400 matches the full 8% deferral, but the match is capped at 4% of pay.
Wrong: $7,200 is only Kyle’s own deferral (8% × $90,000) and ignores the employer match.
Wrong: $3,600 is only the employer match and leaves out Kyle’s own deferral.
Correct: his deferral is 8% × 90,000 = $7,200; the match is 100% of the first 4% (4% × 90,000 = $3,600); total = 7,200 + 3,600 = $10,800.

questions.q: Dana’s plan offers a Roth 401(k) feature. She defers $3,000 to her regular 401(k) and $2,000 to the Roth account. Her employer matches 50% of all her deferrals. Where is the employer’s $2,500 match deposited?
o: Entirely in the Roth 401(k) account
Split 60% regular and 40% Roth
Entirely in the regular 401(k) account
Into a separate Roth IRA for Dana
w: Wrong: Roth 401(k) accounts accept employee deferrals only.
Wrong: the match is not allocated proportionally; employer money is never placed in the Roth account.
Correct: only employee contributions go into the Roth account; every employer match goes to the regular 401(k).
Wrong: an employer match to a 401(k) stays in the plan and is not moved to an individual IRA.

questions.q: For exam purposes, a Keogh plan is available to which of the following?
o: Self-employed individuals
Employees of any corporation with 100 or fewer workers
Government employees
Employees of public schools
w: Correct: a Keogh (HR-10) is for the self-employed and owners of unincorporated businesses.
Wrong: small corporate employers would use SIMPLE or SEP arrangements, not Keogh plans.
Wrong: government employees may use 457(b) plans.
Wrong: public school employees participate in 403(b) plans, not Keogh plans.

questions.q: Which statement about a SEP-IRA is TRUE?
o: Employees may defer their own salary into it
Only the employer may contribute, and the same percentage must be given to all eligible employees
It is required for any business with more than 100 employees
The employer must contribute every year regardless of profit
w: Wrong: employee contributions are not allowed in a SEP-IRA; only the employer contributes.
Correct: SEP contributions come from the employer alone and must be the same percentage for all eligible employees.
Wrong: a SEP is never required and is typically used by small businesses.
Wrong: SEPs are at the employer’s option and are never required.

questions.q: A SIMPLE IRA is best described as which of the following?
o: A plan for self-employed individuals only
A plan for companies of any size where only employees contribute
A plan for companies with 100 or fewer employees, with required employer contributions and optional employee deferrals
A plan for nonprofit organizations with required employee deferrals
w: Wrong: self-employed persons are served by a Keogh plan for exam purposes.
Wrong: employer contributions are required, and the plan has a size cap of 100 employees.
Correct: SIMPLE IRAs target small employers with 100 or fewer eligible employees and require employer contributions.
Wrong: nonprofits use 403(b) plans, and SIMPLE employee deferrals are optional.

questions.q: What is the principal feature that distinguishes a 401(k) from a pure profit-sharing plan?
o: The 401(k) is not covered by ERISA
The 401(k) has no vesting schedule
The 401(k) is a defined benefit plan
The 401(k) gives employees the option to contribute their own salary
w: Wrong: both plan types are ERISA-qualified plans.
Wrong: vesting applies to employer contributions in both plans.
Wrong: both a 401(k) and a profit-sharing plan are defined contribution plans.
Correct: a 401(k) adds the employee’s elective deferral to the employer contribution found in a profit-sharing plan.

questions.q:
Which of the following may sponsor a 457(b) plan?

I. A state government
II. A local government
III. A tax-exempt 501(c) organization
IV. A private for-profit manufacturer
o: I, II and III only
I and II only
III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
w: Correct: 457(b) plans are sponsored by state or local government entities and tax-exempt 501(c) organizations, but not by for-profit corporations.
Wrong: this leaves out tax-exempt 501(c) organizations, which are also permitted sponsors.
Wrong: a for-profit manufacturer would use a 401(k), and this pair also excludes governments.
Wrong: private for-profit companies cannot sponsor a 457(b) plan.

questions.q: A senior executive is covered by a non-qualified deferred compensation arrangement funded by her company. The company then goes bankrupt. What is the most accurate statement about her benefits?
o: They are protected in full because the plan is covered by ERISA vesting rules
The plan assets may be claimed by creditors, so she faces credit risk
They are guaranteed by the insurance company managing the general account
They convert automatically into a rollover IRA
w: Wrong: non-qualified plans are not ERISA-covered, so ERISA vesting protections do not apply.
Correct: non-qualified plan assets are not protected in bankruptcy and creditors can claim them, which is the credit risk of these plans.
Wrong: the general account of an insurer relates to fixed insurance products, not to a corporate non-qualified plan.
Wrong: nothing converts the arrangement into an IRA; she is simply an unsecured claimant against the company.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a non-qualified plan to the employer?
o: The employer can choose which employees participate
The plan avoids nondiscrimination testing
There is no limit on the amount that can be contributed
The company receives an immediate tax deduction when it funds the plan
w: Wrong: selecting participants is a stated advantage of non-qualified plans.
Wrong: because the plan is not ERISA-covered, it avoids nondiscrimination tests.
Wrong: non-qualified plans have no limit on contributions.
Correct: contributions are after-tax and non-deductible; the company generally deducts only when benefits are distributed.

questions.q: A company contributes a total of $350,000 to a non-qualified plan for its CFO. At retirement the account is worth $520,000 and she takes the entire amount. How much is taxed to her as ordinary income?
w: Correct: contributions were after-tax, so only the growth is taxed: 520,000 − 350,000 = $170,000.
Wrong: $520,000 would be taxable only if contributions had been pre-tax, as in a qualified plan.
Wrong: $350,000 is the after-tax basis, which comes out untaxed rather than being the taxable amount.
Wrong: the growth is taxed on distribution in a non-qualified plan; only Roth-type accounts are tax-free.

questions.q: Which of the following individuals is eligible to make a contribution to a traditional IRA?
o: A retiree whose only income is dividends and interest
A college student who earned $3,000 from a part-time job
A retiree whose only income is a corporate pension
A landlord whose only income is capital gains from stock sales
w: Wrong: dividends and interest are investment income, which cannot be contributed to an IRA.
Correct: wages from a job are earned income, and there is no minimum age to contribute.
Wrong: pension income is not earned income and cannot fund an IRA.
Wrong: capital gains are investment income, so a person with only gains cannot contribute.

questions.q: Harry, age 24, earned $4,000 from a part-time job this year and has no other income. What is the maximum he may contribute to a traditional IRA for the year?
w: Wrong: $7,500 is the dollar limit, but Harry may contribute only the lesser of that and his earned income.
Wrong: $3,000 does not correspond to any limit; the cap is 100% of earned income.
Correct: the limit is the lesser of $7,500 or 100% of earned income, and $4,000 is lower.
Wrong: $8,600 includes the catch-up for age 50 or older, which Harry does not qualify for.

questions.q: Walter, age 54, earns $120,000 a year at a company with no retirement plan. Using the 2026 limits in this chapter, what is the maximum he can contribute to his IRA for the year?
w: Wrong: $7,500 is the base limit and omits the $1,100 catch-up available at age 50 or older.
Wrong: the limit is the lesser of the dollar cap or earned income, so 100% of salary does not apply.
Wrong: $9,700 overstates the limit by adding the catch-up twice or inventing a larger catch-up.
Correct: the base limit is $7,500 and age 50 or older adds $1,100, for 7,500 + 1,100 = $8,600.

questions.q: Ravi, age 52, earns all of the $90,000 of his household’s income. His wife Priya, age 48, has no compensation. What is the most that can be contributed to both IRAs combined for the year?
w: Wrong: $8,600 covers only Ravi’s own IRA and ignores the spousal IRA for Priya.
Correct: Ravi may put in 7,500 + 1,100 = $8,600; Priya, under 50, gets a spousal IRA of $7,500; total = $16,100.
Wrong: $15,000 assumes neither spouse can use a catch-up, but Ravi is over 50.
Wrong: $17,200 gives both spouses the catch-up, but Priya is only 48.

questions.q: Priya, age 38, earned $50,000 and contributed $9,000 to her IRA for the year. She does not withdraw the excess. What penalty applies?
w: Wrong: $900 applies 10% to the whole $9,000 contribution, using the wrong rate and the wrong base.
Wrong: $150 would be 10% of the excess, which is the early-withdrawal rate rather than the excess-contribution rate.
Correct: the excess is 9,000 − 7,500 = $1,500, and the penalty is 6% × 1,500 = $90.
Wrong: $1,500 is the excess amount itself, not the penalty on it.

questions.q: A taxpayer wants to make an IRA contribution for tax year 2024. By what date must it be made?
o: April 15, 2025
December 31, 2024
December 31, 2025
w: Correct: IRA contributions are due by the due date of the next federal return, usually April 15 of the following year.
Wrong: the deadline is not the end of the tax year; the contribution window extends past it.
Wrong: no June deadline exists for IRA contributions.
Wrong: waiting until the end of the next calendar year goes well past the tax filing deadline.

questions.q:
Which of the following investments are prohibited in an IRA?

I. Fixed life insurance
II. Antiques and most collectibles
III. Uncovered call options
IV. Corporate bonds
o: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV
w: Wrong: this omits uncovered calls, which are among the risky options positions prohibited in IRAs.
Wrong: corporate bonds are permitted in IRAs, so item IV cannot be prohibited.
Correct: fixed life insurance, antiques and collectibles, and uncovered options are prohibited, while bonds are allowed.
Wrong: item IV is wrong because bonds, stocks, mutual funds and ETFs are all permitted IRA investments.

questions.q: Jordan earns $200,000 and his employer offers no retirement plan, so his traditional IRA contributions are tax-deductible. The employer then introduces a company plan that Jordan is eligible for. What is the effect on Jordan’s traditional IRA contributions?
o: They can only be made after-tax because his income exceeds the threshold
They are no longer permitted
They remain pre-tax because he earns his income from one employer
They convert to Roth contributions automatically
w: Correct: eligible for a corporate plan with income above the threshold, contributions become after-tax (non-deductible).
Wrong: contributions are still permitted; only their tax-deductibility changes.
Wrong: deductibility depends on plan eligibility and income, not on the number of employers.
Wrong: nothing converts automatically; the account stays a traditional IRA with non-deductible contributions.

questions.q: Ann made after-tax (non-deductible) contributions totaling $30,000 to her traditional IRA over the years. At age 62 the account is worth $50,000 and she withdraws all of it. How much is taxed as ordinary income?
w: Wrong: $50,000 would be taxable only if every contribution had been pre-tax.
Correct: only the amount in excess of basis is taxed: 50,000 − 30,000 = $20,000.
Wrong: $30,000 is her basis, which comes out without additional income tax.
Wrong: tax-free treatment belongs to qualified Roth distributions, and the earnings here are taxable.

questions.q: At what age may an owner begin taking distributions from a traditional IRA without the 10% early withdrawal penalty?
w: Wrong: age 55 does not end the penalty; withdrawals before 59½ are penalized unless an exception applies.
Wrong: age 65 is not the penalty-free threshold; the cutoff is 59½.
Wrong: 62 is not a threshold used for IRA distribution penalties.
Correct: withdrawals before 59½ face a 10% penalty unless an exception applies.

questions.q: At age 44, Leo withdraws $25,000 of pre-tax money from his traditional IRA to buy a boat. No exception applies. What is the early withdrawal penalty?
w: Wrong: $1,500 results from using 6%, which is the excess-contribution penalty rate.
Wrong: $6,250 uses 25%, the missed-RMD excise tax rate, which does not apply here.
Correct: the early withdrawal penalty is 10% of the amount withdrawn: 10% × 25,000 = $2,500, in addition to ordinary income tax.
Wrong: $25,000 is the withdrawal itself; the penalty is only a percentage of it.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman withdraws money from her traditional IRA. For which of the following uses would the 10% early withdrawal penalty NOT apply?
o: Paying tuition for her grandchild
Taking a vacation
Buying a vacation home
Funding a new business
w: Correct: education expenses for the owner, spouse, children and grandchildren are an exception to the penalty.
Wrong: a vacation is not among the exceptions, so the penalty would apply.
Wrong: only a first-time home purchase (up to $10,000) is excepted, not a second property.
Wrong: starting a business is not a listed exception to the penalty.

questions.q: Marcus, age 40, withdraws $18,000 from his deductible traditional IRA to buy his first home. The first-time homebuyer exception is limited to $10,000. Assuming no other exception applies, what penalty is due?
w: Wrong: the exception covers only the first $10,000, so the excess is still penalized.
Wrong: $1,800 applies the penalty to the entire withdrawal, ignoring the exception.
Wrong: $1,000 is 10% of the excepted $10,000, which is exactly the portion that escapes the penalty.
Correct: the amount above the limit is 18,000 − 10,000 = $8,000, and 10% × 8,000 = $800.

questions.q: Nora, age 50, receives a check from her IRA custodian in order to move her account to a new provider. She deposits the funds into the new IRA 75 days later. What is the likely result?
o: The transfer is fully tax-free because rollovers have no deadline
The transfer qualifies only if completed within 60 days, so she may face tax and an early withdrawal penalty
Only the 6% excess contribution penalty applies
She owes a 25% excise tax
w: Wrong: rollovers do have a deadline, and missing it creates tax consequences.
Correct: a rollover must be completed within 60 days; at 75 days she risks ordinary income tax and the 10% penalty since she is under 59½.
Wrong: 6% is the penalty for excess contributions, which is a different problem.
Wrong: the 25% excise tax applies to missed required minimum distributions.

questions.q: Elena will turn 73 on June 6, 2027, and has only a traditional IRA. By which date must she take her first required minimum distribution?
o: December 31, 2027
April 15, 2028
April 1, 2028
December 31, 2028
w: Wrong: December 31 of the year she turns 73 is earlier than the required beginning date.
Wrong: April 15 is the IRA contribution deadline, not the RMD date.
Correct: the first RMD is due by April 1 of the year following the year the owner turns 73.
Wrong: later RMDs are due by December 31, but the first one is due by April 1.

questions.q: Thomas’s RMD for the year was $20,000, but he took only $8,000 and did not correct it in the following two years. What excise tax applies?
w: Wrong: $800 applies 10% to the amount actually taken, which is neither the shortfall nor the rate.
Wrong: $1,200 would be 10% of the shortfall, the reduced rate available only if corrected within two years.
Wrong: $5,000 applies 25% to the full RMD instead of just the shortfall.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about required minimum distributions are TRUE?

I. The RMD is based on the account value and the owner’s life expectancy
II. An owner may withdraw more than the required amount
III. Roth IRA owners must take RMDs during their lifetime
IV. Missing an RMD triggers a 25% excise tax on the shortfall
o: I, II and IV only
I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
w: Correct: RMDs depend on balance and life expectancy, can be exceeded, and a shortfall draws a 25% excise tax; Roth IRAs have no lifetime RMDs.
Wrong: this leaves out item IV, since a missed RMD carries a 25% excise tax.
Wrong: item III is false because Roth IRAs require no RMDs during the owner’s lifetime.
Wrong: item III is false, so any choice containing it is incorrect.

questions.q: Walt and Bea, both 66, are retired. Walt earns $6,000 from a part-time job, which is the couple’s only compensation. Walt has already contributed $5,000 to his own IRA for the year. What is the most that may still be contributed to an IRA for Bea?
w: Wrong: $3,600 is merely the room left under Walt’s $8,600 cap, ignoring that the couple’s $6,000 of compensation limits total contributions.
Correct: combined contributions cannot exceed combined earned income of $6,000, so 6,000 − 5,000 already contributed leaves $1,000.
Wrong: $7,500 ignores that total contributions cannot exceed the $6,000 of earned income.
Wrong: $8,600 is the full limit with catch-up, but it is capped by the couple’s compensation.

questions.q: Which statement about a Roth IRA is TRUE?
o: Contributions are tax-deductible
Anyone may contribute regardless of income
The owner must take RMDs beginning at age 73
Qualified distributions, including the growth, are tax-free
w: Wrong: Roth contributions are never deductible; they go in after tax.
Wrong: Roth contributions are available only to taxpayers whose income is below a limit.
Wrong: Roth IRAs have no RMDs during the owner’s lifetime.
Correct: qualified Roth distributions are completely tax-free, growth included.

questions.q:
Which of the following are features of a Roth IRA?

I. Contributions are made with after-tax dollars
II. Contribution eligibility is limited by income
III. RMDs must begin at age 73
IV. The same prohibited investments apply as in a traditional IRA
o: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
w: Wrong: this omits item IV, as a Roth is subject to the same prohibited investments as a traditional IRA.
Correct: Roth contributions are after-tax, income-limited, and subject to the same prohibited investments; no lifetime RMDs apply.
Wrong: item III is false because Roth IRAs have no lifetime RMDs.
Wrong: item III is false, which eliminates any option containing it.

questions.q: Ben, age 66, opened his first Roth IRA on November 3, 2019. When is the earliest date a distribution of his earnings becomes fully tax-free?
o: January 1, 2024
November 3, 2024
January 1, 2025
December 31, 2023
w: Correct: 2019 is year 1, 2020 year 2, 2021 year 3, 2022 year 4, 2023 year 5, so distributions on or after January 1, 2024 qualify (he is already over 59½).
Wrong: the five-year clock starts with the first tax year, not the exact opening date, so waiting until November 2024 is unnecessary.
Wrong: this waits an extra year; the fifth year ends December 31, 2023.
Wrong: December 31, 2023 is still within the fifth tax year, not after it.

questions.q: Alicia, age 45, opened a Roth IRA three years ago. She becomes disabled and withdraws a portion that includes both her contributions and earnings. Which statement is correct?
o: Everything is tax-free because she is disabled
She owes the 10% penalty on the entire withdrawal
The 10% penalty is waived because of disability, but the earnings portion is taxable since the five-year period is not met
Her contributions are taxable and the earnings are tax-free
w: Wrong: disability waives only the penalty; earnings remain taxable when the five-year test is not met.
Wrong: the disability exception removes the 10% penalty.
Correct: with a valid exception the penalty is waived, but earnings are taxed because the account is under five years old.
Wrong: contributions were already taxed and come out tax-free; the earnings are the taxable part here.

questions.q: Carl, age 74, and Dolores, age 67, are a retired couple. Both have earned income from consulting, but their total income is above the Roth IRA income limit. Which statement is correct?
o: Both can contribute to a traditional IRA, but not to a Roth IRA
Both can contribute, but only to a Roth IRA
Neither can contribute to any IRA
Only Dolores can contribute because Carl is past age 73
w: Correct: traditional IRAs have no income limit on contributing (only deductibility is affected) and no age limit, while the Roth has an income limit.
Wrong: their income is above the Roth limit, so Roth contributions are not allowed.
Wrong: both have earned income and traditional IRA contributions are allowed at any age.
Wrong: there is no age cutoff for contributing to a traditional IRA when the person has earned income.

questions.q: When are required minimum distributions triggered for a Roth IRA?
o: April 1 after the owner turns 73
Upon the death of the owner
Never, even after the owner’s death
Age 59½
w: Wrong: this date applies to traditional IRAs, not Roth IRAs.
Correct: Roth IRAs have no lifetime RMDs; the RMD requirement begins at the owner’s death.
Wrong: Roth IRAs have no RMDs during the owner’s life, but the requirement is triggered at death.
Wrong: 59½ is relevant to penalty-free withdrawals, not RMDs.

questions.q: Sam, age 40, earns $100,000. For the year he contributes $4,000 to a traditional IRA and $4,000 to a Roth IRA. Assuming the Roth is open to him, what penalty applies to the excess contribution?
w: Wrong: contribution limits apply to all IRAs in aggregate, so he has exceeded the limit.
Wrong: $48 results from treating $800 as the excess, which has no basis in the numbers.
Correct: total is $8,000 against a $7,500 limit, an excess of $500; 6% × 500 = $30.
Wrong: $80 applies 10% to the $800 or uses the wrong rate; the excess rate is 6%.

questions.q: Annuities are often said to protect against which risk?
o: Dying too soon
Rising interest rates
Market declines in bonds
Living too long and running out of savings
w: Wrong: protection against dying too soon is the purpose of life insurance.
Wrong: interest rate risk is not the purpose of annuity contracts.
Wrong: annuities, especially variable ones, do not eliminate market risk.
Correct: an annuity pays an income guaranteed for life, protecting against outliving savings.

questions.q: Dr. Marsh retires next month and wants a lifetime monthly income of a set dollar amount, with every payment backed by the insurance company. Which product best fits?
o: Deferred variable annuity
Deferred fixed annuity
Immediate variable annuity
Immediate fixed annuity
w: Wrong: a deferred annuity delays payments, and variable payments are not fixed in amount.
Wrong: deferred annuities delay payments, but Paula needs income to start in two months.
Wrong: variable payouts move with performance, so a set dollar amount is not guaranteed.
Correct: an immediate fixed annuity starts paying soon and the insurer guarantees every payment.

questions.q: An investor wants 70% of her annuity premium to earn a guaranteed rate and 30% placed in non-guaranteed stock and bond funds. How can the insurer structure this?
o: 100% in the general account
70% in the separate account and 30% in the general account
70% in the general account and 30% in the separate account
100% in the separate account
w: Wrong: general account assets provide guarantees and would not give Ned the stock and bond fund exposure.
Wrong: this reverses the allocation; separate-account money carries market risk and has no guarantees.
Correct: guaranteed money belongs in the general account and market-based funds in the separate account.
Wrong: separate account assets carry no guarantees, so none of her money would be guaranteed.

questions.q: A representative who sells only fixed annuities needs which license?
o: A Series 7 registration
An insurance license only
Both insurance and securities licenses
An investment adviser registration
w: Wrong: fixed annuities are not securities, so no securities registration is required.
Correct: the insurer, not the buyer, carries the investment risk, so the product falls outside securities law and only an insurance license is needed.
Wrong: both licenses are needed for variable annuities, which are securities.
Wrong: selling a fixed annuity does not require an adviser registration.

questions.q: For regulatory purposes, what is the separate account of a variable annuity treated as?
o: An investment company subject to the Investment Company Act of 1940
A bank subject to Glass-Steagall provisions
A tax-exempt charitable trust
A hedge fund under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940
w: Correct: the separate account is treated as an investment company and must register under the 1940 Act, much like a mutual fund.
Wrong: the separate account is not regulated as a bank.
Wrong: tax status is not what determines how the separate account is regulated.
Wrong: its manager falls under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, but the account itself is an investment company.

questions.q: A guaranteed investment contract (GIC) offered by an insurance company is most like which of the following?
o: A common stock subaccount
A mutual fund with variable returns
A time deposit with guaranteed interest and principal for a fixed period
A Roth IRA
w: Wrong: stock subaccounts belong to the separate account and carry market risk.
Wrong: a GIC has guaranteed returns, unlike a variable mutual fund.
Correct: a GIC is a general-account contract that functions like a time deposit with a guaranteed rate and return of principal.
Wrong: a Roth IRA is an individual retirement account, not an insurance contract.

questions.q: What is the greatest risk of owning a fixed annuity?
o: Credit risk of the stock market
Purchasing power risk
Reinvestment of accumulation units
Liquidity risk of the separate account
w: Wrong: fixed annuities are not invested in stocks by the owner, and the insurer bears investment risk.
Correct: a fixed payout can lose buying power as prices rise, which is purchasing power risk.
Wrong: accumulation units exist only in variable annuities.
Wrong: fixed annuities use the general account, not the separate account.

questions.q: Lena invested a total of $140,000 in a variable annuity. During the accumulation phase the contract value fell to $115,000, and Lena then died. What does her beneficiary receive?
w: Wrong: the current value is lower than the amount contributed, so the guarantee applies.
Wrong: $255,000 adds the two numbers together, which is not how the benefit works.
Wrong: $25,000 is merely the loss in value, not a payout.
Correct: the guaranteed death benefit is the greater of current value or amount contributed, so 140,000 beats 115,000.

questions.q: What happens to the accumulation units when a variable annuity is annuitized?
o: They are swapped for a set count of annuity units whose value determines each payment
They are converted into fixed dollar payments that never change
They are cancelled and replaced by a guaranteed interest rate
They are transferred to the general account
w: Correct: accumulation units become a set number of annuity units; the unit value changes, so payments vary while continuing for life.
Wrong: variable annuity payments fluctuate because annuity unit values change.
Wrong: no guaranteed interest rate replaces them in a variable annuity.
Wrong: variable annuity assets stay in the separate account.

questions.q: An annuitant chooses a life annuity with a 15-year period certain. She dies after receiving payments for 9 years. For how many more years will the beneficiary receive payments?
o: 6 years
0 years
9 years
15 years
w: Correct: the guarantee lasts 15 years in total, and 15 − 9 = 6 years remain for the beneficiary.
Wrong: the beneficiary is protected during the period certain, so payments continue after death in this case.
Wrong: 9 years is how long she already received payments, not what remains.
Wrong: the full 15 years would apply only if she had died before receiving any payments.

questions.q: A variable annuity has a surrender charge schedule of 8%, 7%, 6%, 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%, 1%, 0% for policy years 1 through 9. During policy year 4 the owner withdraws $25,000 before annuitization. What surrender charge applies?
w: Wrong: $1,000 uses 4%, which is the year-5 rate rather than the year-4 rate.
Wrong: $1,750 uses 7%, the year-2 rate.
Wrong: $1,500 uses 6%, the year-3 rate.
Correct: year 4 is 5%, and 5% × 25,000 = $1,250.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a variable annuity surrender charge?
o: To pay the annual premium tax
To allow the insurer to recoup sales commissions paid to the registered representative
To fund the death benefit
To reimburse the SEC for registration
w: Wrong: surrender charges are not a premium tax.
Correct: they are back-end sales charges that let the insurer recover the commissions paid when the product was sold.
Wrong: the death benefit is an insurance feature, not funded by surrender charges.
Wrong: surrender charges have no connection to SEC registration costs.

questions.q:
Which of the following apply to a variable annuity?

I. It must be registered with the SEC
II. It must be sold with a prospectus
III. It may be sold by a representative holding only an insurance license
IV. The seller needs both insurance and securities licenses
o: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
III and IV only
w: Wrong: this leaves out the dual-license requirement, which also applies.
Wrong: item III is false because an insurance license alone is enough only for fixed annuities.
Correct: variable annuities are securities, requiring SEC registration, a prospectus, and both insurance and securities licenses.
Wrong: item III contradicts item IV, and the two cannot both be correct.

questions.q: Greg paid $80,000 of after-tax money into a variable annuity. At age 65 he withdraws the entire contract value of $130,000. How much is taxable as ordinary income?
w: Wrong: $130,000 would be fully taxable only if the contributions had been pre-tax.
Correct: tax is due on the difference between value and basis: 130,000 − 80,000 = $50,000.
Wrong: $80,000 is his basis, which is returned without additional income tax.
Wrong: the earnings in an annuity are taxable when withdrawn, so some amount is taxed.

questions.q: Beth’s 403(b) tax-sheltered annuity was funded entirely with pre-tax deferrals. At age 62 she withdraws $40,000. How is the withdrawal taxed?
o: Only the growth is taxable
None of it is taxable
The entire $40,000 is taxed as long-term capital gains
The entire $40,000 is taxed as ordinary income
w: Wrong: taxing only growth applies where contributions were after-tax, but hers were pre-tax.
Wrong: pre-tax money has never been taxed, so distributions are fully taxable.
Wrong: distributions are never taxed as capital gains.
Correct: an annuity inside a qualified plan funded pre-tax has no basis, so all distributions are ordinary income.

questions.q: Before a variable annuity sale, the customer must be informed of all of the following EXCEPT:
o: A guarantee that the subaccounts will outperform fixed annuity rates
The tax penalty on distributions before age 59½
Market risk associated with the product
Potential surrender charges and the surrender period
w: Correct: no such guarantee exists, and a rep may not promise it; subaccount returns are not guaranteed.
Wrong: the 59½ tax penalty is a required disclosure.
Wrong: market risk must be explained because the investor bears it.
Wrong: surrender period and charges are required disclosures under the suitability rule.

questions.q: A client’s objectives have changed and she wishes to move from her current annuity contract into a different annuity contract with another insurer. What is true of a 1035 exchange?
o: It avoids both taxes and surrender charges
It is taxable on all earnings but penalty-free
It is tax-free, although surrender charges may still apply
It is only permitted for fixed annuities
w: Wrong: avoiding taxes does not mean avoiding surrender charges.
Wrong: the exchange itself is not a taxable event.
Correct: a 1035 exchange avoids tax liability, but the old contract’s surrender charges can still be assessed.
Wrong: an exchange can be made between variable annuity contracts as well.

questions.q: Which statement about 529 college savings plans is TRUE?
o: Contributions are tax-deductible on the federal return
The contributor must have wages in the year the money goes in
An investor may open a plan in any state, and the beneficiary need not attend school there
Only parents may open a plan
w: Wrong: contributions are made with after-tax dollars at the federal level.
Wrong: no earned income is required to contribute to a 529.
Correct: an individual can open a plan in any state, regardless of where the beneficiary studies.
Wrong: any adult may open one, and the beneficiary need not be a relative.

questions.q: The owner of a 529 plan for her daughter wants to change the beneficiary without tax consequences. Which of the following is NOT an acceptable new beneficiary?
o: The daughter’s brother
The daughter’s cousin
The owner herself, using the funds for qualified education expenses
The daughter’s unrelated classmate
w: Wrong: a sibling is a family member, so the change is permitted without tax consequences.
Wrong: a cousin is a relative of the current beneficiary, so the change is allowed.
Wrong: a parent can be the beneficiary as long as the money goes to qualified education expenses.
Correct: a tax-free change of beneficiary is limited to relatives of the current beneficiary.

questions.q: A student enrolled full-time uses 529 plan funds. Which of the following is NOT a qualified education expense?
o: A car for commuting to campus
Required textbooks
Technology fees required by the school
Tuition
w: Correct: transportation costs are not qualified education expenses.
Wrong: books required by the institution are qualified.
Wrong: technology fees required by the school are qualified.
Wrong: tuition is a core qualified expense.

questions.q: Kai is enrolled in college only one course per semester, which is less than half-time. His parents want to pay his off-campus rent from a 529 plan. How are these room and board payments treated?
o: They are qualified up to any amount
They qualify only if Kai carries at least a half-time load, and only up to the school’s allowance
They are always qualified if the school is accredited
They are never qualified for any student
w: Wrong: room and board is qualified only within the school’s allowance and when the half-time test is met.
Correct: room and board qualifies only for students enrolled at least half-time, limited to the institution’s room and board allowance, so Kai’s rent would not qualify.
Wrong: accreditation does not remove the half-time requirement.
Wrong: room and board can qualify for students enrolled at least half-time.

questions.q: Omar’s 529 plan holds $60,000, of which $40,000 was his after-tax contributions. He withdraws the entire balance for a purpose that is not a qualified education expense. What is the 10% federal penalty?
w: Wrong: non-qualified distributions are subject to the 10% federal penalty on the earnings.
Wrong: $4,000 applies 10% to the contributions, which come back untaxed.
Correct: earnings are 60,000 − 40,000 = $20,000, which is taxed as ordinary income, and the penalty is 10% × 20,000 = $2,000.
Wrong: $6,000 applies 10% to the whole balance, but the penalty applies to the earnings portion.

questions.q: A representative is selling a 529 plan sponsored by a state other than the customer’s state of residence. When must the representative disclose potential out-of-state tax consequences?
o: Within 30 days after the sale
At the first distribution
Only if the customer asks
At or prior to the sale
w: Wrong: disclosure after the sale does not satisfy the MSRB requirement.
Wrong: waiting until the first distribution is too late for the investor to decide.
Wrong: the disclosure is mandatory, not dependent on the customer asking.
Correct: MSRB rules require disclosure at or prior to the sale of an out-of-state 529 plan.

questions.q:
Which statements about the taxation of 529 plans are TRUE?

I. Contributions go in with after-tax money for federal purposes
II. Some states allow a deduction for contributions
III. Earnings withdrawn for non-qualified purposes face a 10% federal penalty
IV. The federal government sets a maximum contribution of $7,500
o: I, II and III only
I and II only
II, III and IV only
I and IV only
w: Correct: contributions are after-tax federally, some states give a deduction, and non-qualified earnings carry income tax plus a 10% penalty.
Wrong: this omits item III, since non-qualified earnings do face the 10% penalty.
Wrong: item IV is false because maximum contributions vary by state, and $7,500 is the IRA limit.
Wrong: this pair omits true items and includes the false item IV.

questions.q: A Coverdell ESA was opened for Tara, who has just turned 30. The account still holds $12,000, and no family member has received a transfer. What happens to the balance?
o: It remains tax-free forever
The earnings become subject to federal income tax plus a 10% penalty
It is automatically rolled into a 529 plan with no tax
It is taxed at capital gains rates
w: Wrong: Coverdell funds must be used or transferred to a family member by age 30.
Correct: unused funds at age 30 are subject to federal income tax plus a 10% penalty.
Wrong: no automatic rollover occurs; a transfer to a family member must be arranged.
Wrong: nothing in the Coverdell rules taxes the balance at capital gains rates; it is taxed as income plus a penalty.

questions.q: Which individual is eligible for an ABLE account?
o: A person who is a veteran with no disability
A person whose disability began at age 48
A person with no disability who is a full-time student
A person whose disability began at age 44
w: Wrong: veteran status alone does not create eligibility; a qualifying disability is required.
Wrong: onset at 48 occurs after the age-46 cutoff.
Wrong: a student without a disability does not qualify; a 529 or Coverdell fits that case.
Correct: eligibility requires a disability that began before age 46.

questions.q:
Under MSRB Rule G-45, underwriters of 529 plans and ABLE programs must submit which information to the MSRB?

I. A description of the plan, including the state and the plan manager
II. Aggregate plan assets, contributions and distributions
III. Investment option information, including expenses and performance
IV. The names of individual account owners
o: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
w: Wrong: investment option information is also required.
Wrong: item IV is not required, and the list leaves out the plan description.
Correct: plan description, aggregate plan data and investment option data are submitted semiannually; individual owner names are not.
Wrong: item IV is false, since the reporting is about the plan, not individual owners.

questions.q: Dev tells a colleague, “I’ll be fully vested in three years.” What does he mean?
o: He will have an unconditional right to all of the employer’s contributions after three years
He becomes eligible to join the plan after three years
He may begin making his own contributions after three years
He can withdraw his own contributions tax-free after three years
w: Correct: vesting is ownership of the employer’s money; once fully vested, it cannot be taken back.
Wrong: eligibility to join is a separate test based on age and service.
Wrong: employees can contribute from the start of participation; vesting concerns the employer’s money.
Wrong: vesting does not concern tax treatment, and his own contributions are his immediately.

questions.q: Which employer is most likely to offer its employees a 403(b) plan?
o: A for-profit software company
A public school district
A privately owned retail chain
A self-employed consultant with no staff
w: Wrong: a for-profit company would typically sponsor a 401(k), not a 403(b).
Correct: 403(b) plans serve public schools, 501(c)(3) charities and certain religious institutions.
Wrong: a for-profit retailer is not an eligible 403(b) sponsor; it could use a 401(k) or SIMPLE IRA.
Wrong: a self-employed person would look to a Keogh plan, not a 403(b).

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a Coverdell ESA with a 529 plan?
o: A Coverdell takes pre-tax contributions while a 529 takes after-tax contributions
A Coverdell has no age deadline while a 529 must be emptied by the beneficiary’s 30th birthday

questions.q: Which pair of accounts follows the same tax pattern of after-tax contributions, tax-free growth and tax-free qualified distributions?
o: A deductible traditional IRA and a 529 plan
A Roth IRA and a 529 plan
A non-qualified corporate plan and an ABLE account
A qualified corporate plan and a Roth IRA
w: Wrong: a deductible IRA is funded with pre-tax money and its distributions are fully taxable.
Correct: both are funded with after-tax money, and qualified withdrawals come out completely tax-free.

questions.q: Lucia, age 61, made her first Roth 401(k) deferral four years ago. She now takes a distribution that includes earnings. How are the earnings treated?
o: They are tax-free because she is older than 59½
They are tax-free because Roth accounts inside a 401(k) are never taxed
They are taxed as capital gains because she is over 59½
They are taxable because five years have not passed since her first Roth deferral
w: Wrong: age alone is not enough; the five-year period must also be satisfied.
Wrong: the Roth feature does not remove the five-year requirement.
Wrong: retirement distributions are taxed as ordinary income, never as capital gains.
